Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UAC-0099 fake-PDF VBScript launching Notepad++ / WinRAR (LUNCHPOKE stage) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Notepad++ side-loading NppExport.dll from a non-Program Files path (LUNCHPOKE) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Notepad++ Plugin Delivers MATCHBOIL.V2 in UAC-0099 Attacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] WinRAR extracting password-protected updater.rar in UAC-0099 chain · [LLM] Recurring scheduled task running RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR persistence, 3-min cadence) · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BURNYBEAR (RemoteLibUpdater.exe) loading MATCHBOIL.V2 InitTest.dll
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
UAC-0099 fake-PDF VBScript launching Notepad++ / WinRAR (LUNCHPOKE stage) AIDelivery High
Hunts the UAC-0099 loader stage where a VBScript disguised as a PDF (wscript.exe/cscript.exe) directly spawns the bundled legitimate Notepad++ 8.8.3 or WinRAR from an extracted directory. Legitimate Notepad++/WinRAR are effectively never launched by a script host, making this parent→child pair high-fidelity for the initial execution. Rationale: wscript/cscript → notepad++.exe|winrar.exe is a parent/child pair with near-zero legitimate occurrence; the article states the fake-PDF VBS 'extract the contents of the archive and launch Notepad++'. Anchored on named binaries, not a generic script-spawn template. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195923/cyber-warfare-2/uac-0099-is-now-hiding-malware-inside-a-fake-notepad-plugin-to-target-ukrainian-organizations.html
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Software packaging/deployment scripts (SCCM, PDQ) that call winrar.exe from a VBS wrapper
  • Legacy admin logon scripts that launch text editors
  • Custom VBS installers bundled by a helpdesk that unpack with WinRAR
  • Portable-app launchers that shell out to notepad++.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\SCCM\\","\\PDQ","deploy") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Windows\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent VBS path and command line; confirm the .vbs sits in a user-writable/extracted dir (Downloads, %TEMP%, random-named folder) and check whether a decoy PDF opened simultaneously. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript/cscript and child trees, and quarantine the source ZIP/VBS and any Evernote.zip. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for NppExport.dll side-loading, winrar.exe extracting updater.rar, and a scheduled task running RemoteLibUpdater.exe every 3 minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("notepad++.exe","winrar.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("notepad++.exe","winrar.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: VBScript Host Spawning Notepad++ or WinRAR (UAC-0099 LUNCHPOKE)
id: 6f2c1a4e-3b7d-4c1a-9e0f-2a5d8c1b7e40
description: Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe launching Notepad++ or WinRAR, as seen in the UAC-0099 fake Notepad++ plugin chain.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fake-notepad-plugin-delivers.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1059.005
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\notepad++.exe'
      - '\winrar.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\wscript.exe OR *\Wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe) @Image:(*\notepad++.exe OR *\Notepad++.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(notepad\+\+|winrar)\.exe$/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("notepad++.exe","winrar.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("notepad++.exe","winrar.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Notepad++ side-loading NppExport.dll from a non-Program Files path (LUNCHPOKE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the DLL side-load core of the UAC-0099 chain: a copy of Notepad++ 8.8.3 running from a randomly-named extracted directory loading a malicious NppExport.dll (LUNCHPOKE) instead of the genuine plugin under Program Files. The pivot is location — legitimate NppExport.dll only ever loads from the installed plugins directory. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious plugin name NppExport.dll plus a location predicate: the genuine plugin only loads from the Program Files Notepad++ plugins folder, so a load from a random extracted directory is the side-load itself. Falcon/Sentinel fall back to notepad++.exe executing outside Program Files since image-load isn't in the provided FDR/Sentinel schema. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-weaponize-notepad-plugins/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable Notepad++ builds run from a USB stick or user profile with a bundled export plugin
  • Developers running a self-compiled Notepad++ from a build/output directory
  • Notepad++ installed per-user under %LOCALAPPDATA% rather than Program Files
  • Software-testing sandboxes that stage Notepad++ in a temp folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Portable","\\Notepad++Portable","\\Dev\\","\\build\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded NppExport.dll and compare to the known-good Notepad++ 8.8.3 plugin hash; inspect its parent directory for winrar.exe, updater.rar and Evernote.zip siblings. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the whole extracted directory (Notepad++ copy + DLL + RAR). 3) Hunt: pivot to any scheduled task launching RemoteLibUpdater.exe and to RemoteLibUpdater.exe loading InitTest.dll.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "notepad++.exe"
| where FileName =~ "NppExport.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"

WinRAR extracting password-protected updater.rar in UAC-0099 chain AIInstallation High
Hunts LUNCHPOKE unpacking the second-stage payload: the bundled legitimate winrar.exe (or rar.exe) invoked to extract the password-protected updater.rar that contains RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR) and InitTest.dll (MATCHBOIL.V2). The archive name updater.rar is a campaign-unique anchor. Rationale: updater.rar is a fixed, campaign-specific archive name named in the article; combining it with the extraction utility yields a very low-noise, article-specific detection for the BURNYBEAR/MATCHBOIL.V2 staging step. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://cyberpress.org/hackers-weaponize-notepad-8-8-3/
ATT&CKT1140 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user coincidentally naming a legitimate archive updater.rar (rare)
  • IT distributing a software 'updater.rar' package via WinRAR
  • Backup tooling archiving to a file that happens to match the name
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Windows\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the winrar.exe parent is notepad++.exe or a script host, and that the -p (password) flag or a random destination directory is present; recover the extracted RemoteLibUpdater.exe / InitTest.dll. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine updater.rar and its extracted contents. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for updater.rar drops from EasySend/Evernote.zip lineage and for the 3-minute RemoteLibUpdater.exe scheduled task.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "updater.rar"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| where CommandLine has "updater.rar"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Recurring scheduled task running RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR persistence, 3-min cadence) AIInstallation High
Hunts the UAC-0099 persistence mechanism where LUNCHPOKE registers a scheduled task that launches RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR) every three minutes. The binary name is campaign-unique and the high execution frequency (many launches/hour, typically via Task Scheduler/svchost) is the distinguishing signal. Rationale: RemoteLibUpdater.exe is a campaign-unique binary named in the article; the >=3 execution threshold captures the article's explicit 'every three minutes' scheduled-task cadence, which no legitimate updater mimics. Sigma omitted because this is a count/threshold aggregation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fake-notepad-plugin-delivers.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named internal updater utility coincidentally called RemoteLibUpdater.exe (unlikely)
  • Security tooling repeatedly relaunching a monitored process during testing
  • A crash-loop of a benign service producing many process starts
Suppression filter
| where not (SampleCmd has_any ("\\Program Files\\") and Parents has_any ("services.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate scheduled tasks on the host (schtasks /query or DeviceEvents) for a task pointing at RemoteLibUpdater.exe with a 3-minute trigger; note whether it launches with no arguments (BURNYBEAR resource-exhaustion path) versus loading InitTest.dll. 2) Contain: disable/delete the scheduled task, kill RemoteLibUpdater.exe, isolate the host, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: correlate to the NppExport.dll side-load and updater.rar extraction, and check for MATCHBOIL.V2 C2 egress from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| summarize Executions=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine), FolderPath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, AccountName, SHA256
| where Executions >= 3  // task fires every 3 minutes -> many launches over the window
| order by Executions desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| summarize Executions=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Parents=make_set(ParentProcessName), SampleCmd=any(CommandLine) by Computer, Account, NewProcessName
| where Executions >= 3  // 3-minute recurrence produces many launches
| order by Executions desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\RemoteLibUpdater.exe OR *\remotelibupdater.exe OR *\REMOTELIBUPDATER.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\RemoteLibUpdater\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count(as=Executions))
| Executions>=3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parents values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="RemoteLibUpdater.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=3
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parents values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="RemoteLibUpdater.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=3
BURNYBEAR (RemoteLibUpdater.exe) loading MATCHBOIL.V2 InitTest.dll AICommand & Control High
Hunts the final loader hand-off: RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR) side-loading InitTest.dll, the modified C#-based MATCHBOIL.V2 loader that fetches secondary payloads. Both the loader binary and the DLL names are campaign-unique, making this a very high-fidelity terminal-stage detection. Rationale: Both RemoteLibUpdater.exe and InitTest.dll are unique names disclosed by CERT-UA/THN; their pairing in a single image-load event is essentially pathognomonic for MATCHBOIL.V2 execution. Falcon/Splunk fall back to the InitTest.dll file drop since image-load isn't in the provided FDR/CIM schema; Sentinel uses the RemoteLibUpdater.exe process-create proxy. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://cyberpress.org/hackers-weaponize-notepad-8-8-3/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate InitTest.dll used by a test harness in a dev environment
  • A security-product module coincidentally sharing the RemoteLibUpdater.exe name
  • EDR-replayed IOC test in a sandbox during purple-team exercises
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitTest.dll and RemoteLibUpdater.exe hashes and the loading directory; check DeviceNetworkEvents from RemoteLibUpdater.exe for MATCHBOIL.V2 C2 or Dropbox WinRAR retrieval. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, delete the 3-minute scheduled task, and quarantine both binaries. 3) Hunt: pivot org-wide on the InitTest.dll/RemoteLibUpdater.exe hashes and on NppExport.dll side-loads to find other compromised hosts.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| where FileName =~ "InitTest.dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Russian Espionage Group Exploited Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Mail and 2FA Codes

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 21 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A Russian state-supported espionage group spent months reading Western mailboxes through a then-unknown flaw in Zimbra's webmail client. The payload goes after the last 90 days of email, the organization's entire email directory, the password saved in the browser and the codes kept for two-factor recovery. Opening the message was enough to start it. The NSA, CISA and partner agencies published

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ZimReaper CVE-2025-66376 payload staging — DNS to js-*.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Zimbra app-specific password 'ZimbraWeb' minted via CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest · [LLM] Zimbra IMAP silently enabled (zimbraPrefImapEnabled = TRUE) for MFA-free mailbox access · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Russian Espionage Group Exploited Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Mail and 2FA Codes
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ZimReaper C2 & mail exfiltration to actor IPs/domains (TGZ upload + DNS exfil) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Zimbra 2FA scratch-code theft via GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP call · [LLM] Zimbra Global Address List brute-force via SearchGalRequest two-character enumeration · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ZimReaper CVE-2025-66376 payload staging — DNS to js-*.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua AIExploitation High
Detects the moment the Zimbra Classic-UI stored XSS (CVE-2025-66376) fires and the svg-onload=eval(atob()) stager reaches the actor's payload-staging subdomains. Endpoints that render a booby-trapped webmail message resolve js-<random>.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua from the user's browser process — the earliest on-host evidence of exploitation. Rationale: Anchored on the two named staging subdomains and the fixed '.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua' label pattern (corroborated by Proofpoint/Unit 42). A workstation browser resolving these = ZimReaper stager fetch, i.e. CVE-2025-66376 exploitation firing on render. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal DNS sinkhole / security appliance pre-resolving IOC feed domains for blocking
  • Threat-intel scanner or sandbox detonation host resolving the domain deliberately
  • Passive DNS / DNS-logging tooling replaying captured queries
  • Researcher validating the IOC on a test host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the endpoint + user; confirm the DNS was browser-initiated (InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser) and that the user runs Zimbra Classic UI. Pull the mailbox and check for an unopened/opened HTML message with fragmented @import + svg onload. 2) Contain: reset the user's Zimbra password, invalidate active webmail sessions, regenerate 2FA scratch codes, and block the domain at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same device/user for GetScratchCodesRequest, CreateAppSpecificPassword 'ZimbraWeb', zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE, and any egress to the nine C2 IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".i.zimbrasoft.com.ua"
    or RemoteUrl in~ ("js-l1wt597cimk.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua","js-26tik3egye4.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort

ZimReaper C2 & mail exfiltration to actor IPs/domains (TGZ upload + DNS exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects endpoints or the Zimbra host communicating with the nine ZimReaper C2 IP addresses or nine actor domains — the channel used to exfiltrate stolen 2FA scratch codes/CSRF token over DNS and to POST 90 days of mailbox contents as a TGZ archive. Straight IOC match on infrastructure confirmed present in both the Unit 42 and Proofpoint indicator lists. Rationale: Uses the nine C2 IPs and nine domains that The Hacker News confirmed appear in BOTH Unit 42's and Proofpoint's indicator lists (shared infrastructure tying CL-STA-1114 to TA488) — high-fidelity IOC match for the mail-TGZ upload and DNS exfil egress. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits

  • Threat-intel enrichment jobs actively probing the IPs
  • VPN/NAT egress collapsing many users behind one srcAddr, inflating hits
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which internal host/user initiated the flow and direction; large outbound bytes to these IPs = probable mailbox TGZ exfil. Check the same host for prior '.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua' DNS. 2) Contain: block all nine IPs and nine domains at perimeter, isolate the involved endpoint, force Zimbra password reset + session invalidation + scratch-code regeneration for the affected mailbox. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host that touched any IOC in 90 days; on the Zimbra server review /opt/zimbra/log/audit.log for GetScratchCodesRequest / CreateAppSpecificPassword 'ZimbraWeb' / zimbraPrefImapEnabled changes tied to those accounts.

Zimbra 2FA scratch-code theft via GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP call AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on Zimbra SOAP GetScratchCodesRequest (ZimbraAccount namespace) in mailbox/audit logs. ZimReaper's gather_2fa_codes stage calls this API from the hijacked webmail session to pull 2FA recovery codes; Proofpoint states the call 'should be close to absent in normal use', making even a single occurrence high-signal. Rationale: GetScratchCodesRequest is the exact SOAP command name (corroborated by Unit 42's gather_2fa_codes stage description) and is explicitly flagged by Proofpoint as an actionable near-zero-baseline alert — no threshold or correlation needed. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits
ATT&CKT1111 T1539
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine end-user viewing their own 2FA recovery/scratch codes in account settings
  • Zimbra admin auditing a user's MFA configuration
  • Automated backup/migration tooling snapshotting account preferences
  • Penetration-test or MFA-reset support workflow
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the target account and the source session/IP issuing the SOAP call; correlate with recent webmail render of a suspicious HTML message and any '.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua' DNS from the user's endpoint. 2) Contain: immediately reset the account password, invalidate active sessions, and regenerate all 2FA scratch codes (the stolen ones survive a password reset). 3) Hunt: search the same session for CreateAppSpecificPassword 'ZimbraWeb', zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE, and SearchGalRequest bursts; pull the originating message for the fragmented @import/svg-onload pattern with Proofpoint's YARA.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "GetScratchCodesRequest"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zimbra app-specific password 'ZimbraWeb' minted via CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a Zimbra app-specific password named 'ZimbraWeb' through the CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest SOAP command. ZimReaper mints this credential to grant IMAP/POP3/SMTP access that bypasses 2FA and survives password resets — the actor's primary persistence mechanism. Rationale: CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest + the literal app name 'ZimbraWeb' are exact strings from the article and Unit 42/Proofpoint; the article's remediation guidance explicitly says to review audit.log for this and delete the ZimbraWeb credential. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits
ATT&CKT1098 T1556.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately creating an app password for a real IMAP/mobile mail client (but rarely named exactly 'ZimbraWeb')
  • Admin provisioning app passwords during a mail-client migration
  • Automation/service account setup requiring app-specific credentials
  • MDM enrollment generating device mail credentials
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the account and whether the user requested any app password; the name 'ZimbraWeb' is the actor's default and is not a normal client name. 2) Contain: delete the ZimbraWeb app-specific password, reset the account password, invalidate sessions, and audit IMAP/POP3/SMTP logins made with it (app passwords survive password resets and skip 2FA). 3) Hunt: check zimbraPrefImapEnabled flips, GetScratchCodesRequest, and outbound IMAP/SMTP from the compromised mailserver to unknown hosts; enumerate all accounts with a ZimbraWeb credential.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest"
    or (SyslogMessage has "CreateAppSpecificPassword" and SyslogMessage has "ZimbraWeb")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zimbra IMAP silently enabled (zimbraPrefImapEnabled = TRUE) for MFA-free mailbox access AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Zimbra account preference zimbraPrefImapEnabled being set to TRUE, observed by Seqrite in the Ukrainian hydrology-agency case. Combined with the minted app-specific password, this lets the actor pull mail over IMAP without 2FA and persists across password resets. Rationale: zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE is the exact preference/value string from the article's Seqrite January case; the article recommends finding accounts with it set that have no business need for IMAP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-espionage-group-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1556 T1114.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User or admin legitimately enabling IMAP for a desktop/mobile mail client
  • Bulk provisioning enabling IMAP org-wide by policy
  • Mail-client migration turning IMAP on for many accounts
  • Helpdesk enabling IMAP at user request
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-reference the account against those with a legitimate IMAP business need and against any ZimbraWeb app-password or GetScratchCodesRequest events on the same account. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, set zimbraPrefImapEnabled back to FALSE, revoke app passwords, reset credentials, and review recent IMAP session logins for the account. 3) Hunt: list all accounts recently flipped to IMAP-enabled and correlate with exploitation-time DNS ('.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua') and C2 IP egress; scope which mailboxes had 90-day mail pulled.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "zimbraPrefImapEnabled" and SyslogMessage has "TRUE"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zimbra Global Address List brute-force via SearchGalRequest two-character enumeration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the high-volume SearchGalRequest activity ZimReaper generates when it brute-forces the Global Address List by querying every two-character combination to dump the full org directory. A single session or host producing hundreds of GAL searches in minutes is well above human autocomplete use. Rationale: SearchGalRequest is the Zimbra SOAP command behind GAL autocomplete; the article specifies ZimReaper queries 'every two-character combination until the whole list comes back', which produces a distinctive volume spike detectable as a threshold on GAL search calls. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits
ATT&CKT1087.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mail-client address-book sync performing many rapid GAL lookups
  • Newsletter/distribution tooling resolving large recipient sets
  • Directory-migration or reporting scripts enumerating the GAL
  • A power user typing many autocomplete queries in a short burst
Suppression filter
| where HostName !in~ ("addressbook-sync-host")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account/session driving the SearchGalRequest volume and whether the queries are systematic short strings (aa, ab, ac…) versus real names; correlate with a recent webmail render of a suspicious message. 2) Contain: if malicious, reset the account, invalidate sessions, and treat the entire GAL as exfiltrated (directory disclosure). 3) Hunt: check the same session for GetScratchCodesRequest, CreateAppSpecificPassword 'ZimbraWeb', and outbound egress to the nine C2 IPs / actor domains; assess which mailboxes were archived to TGZ.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "SearchGalRequest"
| summarize Requests = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage) by HostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Requests > 200   // ZimReaper enumerates ~1,296 two-char combos; normal user GAL autocomplete is far below 200 per 5min
| order by Requests desc
source:linux.syslog SearchGalRequest
APPLICATION
index=zimbra "SearchGalRequest"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as Requests min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by _time host
| where Requests > 200
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - Requests
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-66376")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-66376")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or SHA1 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or MD5 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or SHA1 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or MD5 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData (msaRAT delivery)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Don’t swing at everything
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msiexec executing MSI masquerading as Windows update from ProgramData · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port by non-browser parent (CDP abuse) · [LLM] Plain-HTTP over port 443 to msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 · [LLM] Browser contacting msaRAT WebRTC signaling relay (workers.dev Cloudflare Worker) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData (msaRAT delivery) AIDelivery High
Hunts msaRAT's initial delivery step where curl.exe pulls an MSI impersonating a Windows update into C:\ProgramData over plain HTTP. Article-specific because it pairs the curl LOLBin with both a .msi extension and a ProgramData drop path — Talos explicitly flags this exact command shape. Rationale: Uses the exact Talos-described command shape (curl + .msi + ProgramData). Two independent sources (BleepingComputer, The Hacker News) confirm curl.exe pulls the MSI into ProgramData, making this high-fidelity rather than a generic ingress-tool-transfer template. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Software packaging/deployment tooling using curl to stage MSI installers in ProgramData
  • IT admin manually downloading a vendor MSI to a ProgramData staging folder
  • RMM/patch-management agents (e.g. Chocolatey, PDQ) that fetch MSIs via curl
  • CI/build agents that pull MSI artifacts into ProgramData for testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pdqdeployrunner.exe","choco.exe","chocolatey.exe","ninite.exe","tacticalrmm.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full curl command line and the source URL/IP; confirm whether the host has legitimate deployment tooling that uses curl, and check the SHA256 of the dropped MSI against Talos IOCs. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the source IP (172.86.126.18) at the firewall, and quarantine the MSI in ProgramData before it is executed by msiexec. 3) Hunt: search the host and peers for subsequent msiexec.exe execution of the ProgramData MSI, chrome.exe/msedge.exe launched with --remote-debugging-port, and outbound connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ProgramData"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".msi" and CommandLine has "ProgramData"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msiexec executing MSI masquerading as Windows update from ProgramData AIInstallation High
Hunts msaRAT's execution step: msiexec launching a curl-dropped MSI from ProgramData whose name impersonates a Windows update/patch, whose install runs a custom action loading a DLL from inside the installer straight into memory. Article-specific via the ProgramData path plus update/patch/KB naming lure. Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed masquerade (MSI posing as a Windows update dropped in ProgramData) reported by Talos and echoed by The Hacker News. Legitimate Windows updates never install from ProgramData via a curl-dropped MSI, so the path+name combination is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party app updaters that stage MSIs in a vendor ProgramData subfolder with 'update' in the name
  • Enterprise patch tooling repackaging updates as MSIs staged in ProgramData
  • Driver/firmware update MSIs (e.g. Dell/HP) named with 'update' running from ProgramData
  • Internal software distribution that names MSIs after KB numbers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pdqdeployrunner.exe","choco.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","dellcommandupdate.exe","hpsupportassistant.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the MSI path/name and its SHA256, and identify the parent process — a curl.exe or unknown ProgramData binary parent is a strong TP signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill/quarantine the msiexec chain; snapshot memory since the custom action loads a DLL directly into memory. 3) Hunt: look for the browser being launched with --remote-debugging-port shortly after, connections to 172.86.126.18:443 and is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev, and stage for possible ransomware pre-encryption behavior.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ProgramData"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","patch","windows","KB")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "ProgramData" and CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has_any ("update","patch","windows","KB")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port by non-browser parent (CDP abuse) AICommand & Control High
Hunts msaRAT driving Chrome or Edge over the Chrome DevTools Protocol by starting the browser with a --remote-debugging-port flag, typically spawned by the malicious loader rather than a user shell. This is the core living-off-the-browser C2 setup Talos describes. Rationale: Talos and multiple write-ups (BleepingComputer, Gridinsoft) confirm msaRAT starts a headless browser and drives it via CDP; the --remote-debugging-port flag is the observable that enables CDP. Excluding legit browser/explorer parents removes the bulk of benign automation while keeping the loader-spawned case. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/msarat-chrome-edge-browser-c2/
ATT&CKT1205 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser testing frameworks (Selenium, Puppeteer, Playwright) launching Chrome with a debug port
  • Developers manually debugging web apps with remote debugging enabled
  • Electron/CEF-based apps that invoke chromium with a debugging port
  • Headless-Chrome PDF/screenshot rendering services spawned by app servers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","selenium.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "playwright"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and its folder path — a parent from ProgramData or an unsigned/unknown binary is a strong TP; check for a co-occurring loopback (127.0.0.1) CDP connection. 2) Contain: isolate the host and terminate the parent loader plus the debug-port browser instance. 3) Hunt: correlate with the same host reaching is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev (WebRTC signaling) and Twilio TURN, and look back for the curl→MSI→msiexec delivery chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","code.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\explorer.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\chrome.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Plain-HTTP over port 443 to msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts msaRAT's evasive delivery channel: unencrypted HTTP to the confirmed C2/staging IP 172.86.126.18 on port 443, which slips past firewalls that trust 443 by number without protocol inspection. Anchored on the confirmed network IOC plus the plaintext-on-443 behavior Talos calls out. Rationale: 172.86.126.18:443 is a confirmed IOC (Talos IOC table, echoed by Help Net Security). Talos specifically notes the traffic is plain HTTP on 443 to bypass port-only firewall rules, so pairing the exact IP with port 443 (and HttpConnectionInspected on 443 as the plaintext behavior) is high-confidence and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195876/malware/chaos-ransomware-deploys-browser-based-msarat-to-evade-network-detection.html
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • If the IP is later reassigned to a benign hosting tenant, unrelated legitimate traffic could hit it
  • Security scanners/threat-intel validation tooling deliberately probing the IOC IP
  • Proxy or gateway appliances logging the connection on behalf of many hosts (source attribution noise)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process (curl.exe or a ProgramData binary is a strong TP) and whether the payload on 443 was HTTP rather than TLS. 2) Contain: block 172.86.126.18 org-wide at egress, isolate any host that connected, and preserve the downloaded MSI. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same hosts for browser --remote-debugging-port launches and DNS/connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev, and sweep the environment for other hosts touching this IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18"
| where RemotePort == 443 or ActionType == "HttpConnectionInspected"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18" and DestinationPort == 443
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
